title: Waste Management & Bioremediation
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned Nigerian university 300L Waste Management & Bioremediation curriculum: solid and liquid waste characterisation, wastewater treatment stages, composting and landfill microbiology, biogas/anaerobic digestion, bioremediation strategies (in situ/ex situ, bioaugmentation, biostimulation), and biodegradation of xenobiotics, oil and heavy metals.

questions.question: Biological Oxygen Demand (BOD) is defined as:
options: The total volume of a wastewater sample
The amount of dissolved oxygen consumed by microorganisms while decomposing organic matter in a water sample over a set period, usually 5 days at 20°C
The amount of oxygen produced by algae in a pond
The concentration of heavy metals in wastewater
questions.correct_answer: The amount of dissolved oxygen consumed by microorganisms while decomposing organic matter in a water sample over a set period, usually 5 days at 20°C
questions.explanation: BOD5 measures the oxygen consumed by aerobic microorganisms as they biodegrade organic matter in a sample over five days at 20°C, and is a standard indicator of the organic pollution load of water or wastewater.

questions.question: Chemical Oxygen Demand (COD) differs from BOD in that COD:
options: Measures only biodegradable organic matter
Measures the total oxygen equivalent required to chemically oxidise both biodegradable and non-biodegradable organic matter, usually using a strong oxidant such as dichromate
Can only be measured using live bacteria
Is always numerically lower than BOD for the same sample
questions.correct_answer: Measures the total oxygen equivalent required to chemically oxidise both biodegradable and non-biodegradable organic matter, usually using a strong oxidant such as dichromate
questions.explanation: COD uses a strong chemical oxidant to oxidise essentially all organic matter (biodegradable and recalcitrant), so it is typically equal to or higher than BOD and gives a faster, broader measure of pollution load than the 5-day BOD test.

questions.question: Primary treatment in a conventional wastewater treatment plant mainly achieves:
options: Complete removal of dissolved organic pollutants by microbial action
Physical removal of large solids and settleable suspended matter by screening and sedimentation
Disinfection of the final effluent
Biological nitrification of ammonia
questions.correct_answer: Physical removal of large solids and settleable suspended matter by screening and sedimentation
questions.explanation: Primary treatment is a physical stage using screens, grit chambers, and sedimentation tanks to remove large debris and settleable solids before the wastewater proceeds to biological (secondary) treatment.

questions.question: Secondary treatment of wastewater relies principally on:
options: Screening out large floating debris
Microbial (biological) degradation of dissolved and colloidal organic matter, e.g. by the activated sludge process or trickling filters
Chlorination alone
Sand filtration only
questions.correct_answer: Microbial (biological) degradation of dissolved and colloidal organic matter, e.g. by the activated sludge process or trickling filters
questions.explanation: Secondary treatment uses aerobic microbial communities, commonly in the activated sludge process or on trickling filter media, to biodegrade dissolved and colloidal organic pollutants remaining after primary treatment.

questions.question: In the activated sludge process, the 'activated sludge' itself refers to:
options: A chemical coagulant added to the wastewater
A flocculent microbial biomass (a mixed community of bacteria, protozoa, and other microorganisms) that is recycled to continuously degrade organic pollutants in incoming wastewater
The final treated effluent released to the environment
The solid residue after incineration of sludge
questions.correct_answer: A flocculent microbial biomass (a mixed community of bacteria, protozoa, and other microorganisms) that is recycled to continuously degrade organic pollutants in incoming wastewater
questions.explanation: Activated sludge is a microbial floc, dominated by bacteria along with protozoa and other microfauna, that is aerated with incoming wastewater to oxidise organic matter, then settled and partly recycled to maintain a high active biomass concentration.

questions.question: In activated sludge secondary clarifiers, protozoa (especially ciliates) are important because their abundance and activity:
options: Have no diagnostic value
Serve as a useful biological indicator of a healthy, well-functioning activated sludge system, since they graze on dispersed bacteria and help clarify the effluent
Always indicate plant failure
Only matter in anaerobic digesters
questions.correct_answer: Serve as a useful biological indicator of a healthy, well-functioning activated sludge system, since they graze on dispersed bacteria and help clarify the effluent
questions.explanation: A diverse, active ciliate protozoan population feeding on free-swimming bacteria is a classic indicator of good activated sludge performance and effluent clarity; their decline or absence signals a process upset.

questions.question: Trickling filters treat wastewater by:
options: Passing wastewater through a bed of coarse medium coated with a microbial biofilm, which degrades organic matter as the liquid trickles over it
Boiling the wastewater to sterilise it
Adding chlorine gas directly to raw sewage
Freezing the wastewater to separate solids
questions.correct_answer: Passing wastewater through a bed of coarse medium coated with a microbial biofilm, which degrades organic matter as the liquid trickles over it
questions.explanation: In a trickling filter, wastewater is sprayed over a bed of rocks or plastic media colonised by an attached microbial biofilm (zoogloea); as the liquid trickles through, the biofilm organisms metabolise dissolved organic matter.

questions.question: Tertiary (advanced) wastewater treatment is aimed at:
options: Removing large solids only
Removing residual nutrients (e.g. nitrogen, phosphorus) and pathogens not eliminated by primary and secondary treatment, to produce a higher-quality effluent
Producing raw sewage from treated water
Skipping biological treatment altogether
questions.correct_answer: Removing residual nutrients (e.g. nitrogen, phosphorus) and pathogens not eliminated by primary and secondary treatment, to produce a higher-quality effluent
questions.explanation: Tertiary treatment polishes secondary effluent further, targeting nutrients that cause eutrophication (nitrogen, phosphorus) and pathogens, often via processes such as nutrient removal, filtration, and disinfection.

questions.question: Anaerobic digestion of sewage sludge or organic waste, used both to stabilise waste and generate biogas, relies on a microbial consortium that ultimately produces:
options: Pure oxygen
Methane (CH4) and carbon dioxide (CO2) as the main biogas products, via sequential hydrolysis, acidogenesis, acetogenesis, and methanogenesis
Only lactic acid
Nitrate as the final product
questions.correct_answer: Methane (CH4) and carbon dioxide (CO2) as the main biogas products, via sequential hydrolysis, acidogenesis, acetogenesis, and methanogenesis
questions.explanation: Anaerobic digestion proceeds through hydrolysis of complex polymers, acidogenesis and acetogenesis to volatile fatty acids and acetate/H2, and finally methanogenesis, in which methanogenic archaea produce methane and CO2 as biogas.

questions.question: Methanogens, the organisms responsible for the final step of anaerobic digestion, are classified as:
options: Fungi
Archaea, strict anaerobes that are highly sensitive to oxygen
Gram-positive bacteria
Protozoa
questions.correct_answer: Archaea, strict anaerobes that are highly sensitive to oxygen
questions.explanation: Methanogens belong to the domain Archaea and are obligate anaerobes that produce methane from substrates such as acetate, CO2/H2, or methylated compounds; even brief oxygen exposure can inhibit or kill them.

questions.question: Composting is best described as a:
options: Purely chemical process requiring no microorganisms
Controlled, largely aerobic biological decomposition of organic solid waste by a succession of microbial communities, producing a stabilised, humus-like product
Method that only works in strictly anaerobic conditions
Physical process of shredding waste with no biodegradation
questions.correct_answer: Controlled, largely aerobic biological decomposition of organic solid waste by a succession of microbial communities, producing a stabilised, humus-like product
questions.explanation: Composting harnesses aerobic microbial decomposition (bacteria, actinomycetes, fungi) of organic waste, passing through mesophilic, thermophilic, and cooling/maturation phases, to yield stable, nutrient-rich compost.

questions.question: During the thermophilic phase of composting, temperatures commonly rise above 55°C mainly because of:
options: External heating by the compost operator
Intense microbial metabolic (exothermic) activity as thermophilic bacteria and actinomycetes rapidly degrade readily available organic matter
Solar radiation alone
Chemical combustion of the waste
questions.correct_answer: Intense microbial metabolic (exothermic) activity as thermophilic bacteria and actinomycetes rapidly degrade readily available organic matter
questions.explanation: Heat generated as a byproduct of vigorous aerobic microbial respiration accumulates within the compost pile, raising internal temperatures into the thermophilic range, which also helps destroy pathogens and weed seeds.

questions.question: An optimal carbon-to-nitrogen (C:N) ratio for efficient composting is generally considered to be around:
questions.explanation: A C:N ratio of roughly 25-30:1 provides microorganisms with sufficient carbon for energy and enough nitrogen for cell growth and protein synthesis; ratios that are much higher slow decomposition, while much lower ratios can cause nitrogen loss as ammonia.

questions.question: In a sanitary landfill, the leachate that percolates through buried waste is of major environmental concern because it:
options: Is always sterile and harmless
Can carry dissolved organic matter, pathogens, and pollutants that may contaminate groundwater if not properly collected and treated
Only contains rainwater
Cannot move through soil
questions.correct_answer: Can carry dissolved organic matter, pathogens, and pollutants that may contaminate groundwater if not properly collected and treated
questions.explanation: Leachate forms as water percolates through decomposing waste, dissolving organic and inorganic contaminants and microorganisms; modern landfills use liners and leachate collection systems to prevent groundwater contamination.

questions.question: Landfill gas, generated by anaerobic decomposition of buried municipal solid waste, is composed predominantly of:
options: Oxygen and nitrogen
Methane and carbon dioxide
Hydrogen sulfide only
Pure hydrogen
questions.correct_answer: Methane and carbon dioxide
questions.explanation: Buried organic waste undergoes anaerobic digestion within the landfill, generating landfill gas that is mainly a mixture of methane (a potent greenhouse gas, sometimes captured for energy) and carbon dioxide.

questions.question: Bioremediation is best defined as:
options: The physical removal of contaminated soil for landfill disposal
The use of living organisms, primarily microorganisms, to degrade, transform, or remove environmental pollutants into less harmful forms
The incineration of hazardous waste
The dilution of pollutants with clean water
questions.correct_answer: The use of living organisms, primarily microorganisms, to degrade, transform, or remove environmental pollutants into less harmful forms
questions.explanation: Bioremediation exploits the natural metabolic capabilities of microorganisms (and sometimes plants) to break down or detoxify pollutants such as hydrocarbons, pesticides, and some heavy metal compounds.

questions.question: In situ bioremediation is distinguished from ex situ bioremediation in that in situ methods:
options: Always require excavating the contaminated material
Treat the contaminated soil or groundwater at its original location, without excavation or removal
Can only be applied to water pollution
Never involve microorganisms
questions.correct_answer: Treat the contaminated soil or groundwater at its original location, without excavation or removal
questions.explanation: In situ bioremediation treats contamination directly at the polluted site (e.g. by injecting nutrients or oxygen into contaminated groundwater), avoiding the cost and disturbance of excavating and moving material, unlike ex situ approaches.

questions.question: Biostimulation, as a bioremediation strategy, involves:
options: Adding non-native, laboratory-grown microorganisms to a contaminated site
Adding nutrients (e.g. nitrogen, phosphorus) or electron acceptors to stimulate the activity of the indigenous, pollutant-degrading microbial population already present at the site
Physically excavating contaminated soil
Sterilising the contaminated site before treatment
questions.correct_answer: Adding nutrients (e.g. nitrogen, phosphorus) or electron acceptors to stimulate the activity of the indigenous, pollutant-degrading microbial population already present at the site
questions.explanation: Biostimulation works by supplying growth-limiting nutrients or electron acceptors/donors to enhance the metabolic activity of the naturally occurring microbial community capable of degrading the pollutant, rather than introducing new organisms.

questions.question: Bioaugmentation, as a bioremediation strategy, differs from biostimulation in that bioaugmentation:
options: Involves only adding fertiliser to soil

Involves deliberately introducing specific, often specially selected or engineered, pollutant-degrading microorganisms to a contaminated site to supplement or replace an inadequate indigenous population
Never requires laboratory preparation of organisms
Is identical to biostimulation
questions.correct_answer: Involves deliberately introducing specific, often specially selected or engineered, pollutant-degrading microorganisms to a contaminated site to supplement or replace an inadequate indigenous population
questions.explanation: Bioaugmentation adds exogenous microbial strains (often enriched or engineered for a specific pollutant) to a site, used when the native microbial community lacks sufficient degradative capacity, in contrast to biostimulation, which boosts existing organisms.

questions.question: Bioventing, an in situ bioremediation technique applied to petroleum-contaminated unsaturated soil, works by:
options: Injecting air (or oxygen) into the subsurface to stimulate aerobic biodegradation of hydrocarbons by indigenous microorganisms
Flooding the site with anaerobic water
Removing soil for offsite incineration
Sealing the contaminated zone with an impermeable liner
questions.correct_answer: Injecting air (or oxygen) into the subsurface to stimulate aerobic biodegradation of hydrocarbons by indigenous microorganisms
questions.explanation: Bioventing supplies oxygen (typically via low-flow air injection wells) to the unsaturated zone, enhancing aerobic microbial degradation of petroleum hydrocarbons in situ, while minimising volatilisation of contaminants.

questions.question: Composting of excavated contaminated soil, mixed with bulking agents and organic amendments to enhance microbial degradation of pollutants, is an example of:
options: In situ bioremediation
Ex situ bioremediation
Chemical oxidation
Phytoextraction
questions.correct_answer: Ex situ bioremediation
questions.explanation: Because the contaminated soil is excavated and treated (e.g. in composting piles or biopiles) away from its original location, this is classified as ex situ bioremediation, even though the underlying process is biological.

questions.question: Alcanivorax and other hydrocarbonoclastic marine bacteria are notable for their role in:
options: Fixing nitrogen in agricultural soils
Degrading crude oil hydrocarbons following marine oil spills, bloomed opportunistically using the spilled oil as a carbon and energy source
Producing antibiotics in industrial fermentation
Causing food spoilage
questions.correct_answer: Degrading crude oil hydrocarbons following marine oil spills, bloomed opportunistically using the spilled oil as a carbon and energy source
questions.explanation: Hydrocarbon-degrading marine bacteria such as Alcanivorax species proliferate rapidly after oil spills, using components of crude oil as carbon and energy sources, and are central to natural attenuation and enhanced bioremediation of marine oil pollution.

questions.question: In bioremediation of oil spills, biosurfactants produced by certain microorganisms aid degradation mainly by:
options: Killing all microorganisms present at the spill site
Emulsifying hydrophobic hydrocarbons, increasing their bioavailability and surface area for microbial attack
Converting oil directly to carbon dioxide without any enzymatic action
Preventing any microbial growth near the spill
questions.correct_answer: Emulsifying hydrophobic hydrocarbons, increasing their bioavailability and surface area for microbial attack
questions.explanation: Biosurfactants reduce interfacial tension and emulsify hydrophobic oil droplets into the aqueous phase, increasing the surface area available for microbial cells and their degradative enzymes to access the hydrocarbons.

questions.question: Bioleaching, applied in mining and sometimes in remediation of metal-contaminated materials, uses acidophilic bacteria such as Acidithiobacillus ferrooxidans to:
options: Immobilise metals permanently as insoluble sulfides
Oxidise sulfide minerals, solubilising metals (e.g. copper) into solution for recovery, or mobilising metals from contaminated matrices
Fix atmospheric nitrogen for plant use
Degrade organic pesticides
questions.correct_answer: Oxidise sulfide minerals, solubilising metals (e.g. copper) into solution for recovery, or mobilising metals from contaminated matrices
questions.explanation: Acidithiobacillus ferrooxidans and related acidophiles oxidise reduced sulfur and iron compounds in sulfide minerals, generating acidic, oxidising conditions that solubilise metals such as copper, a process exploited commercially in bioleaching.

questions.question: Biosorption, one mechanism by which microorganisms remove heavy metals from contaminated water, refers to:
options: Active, energy-dependent metabolic uptake of metals only
Passive binding of metal ions to functional groups on microbial cell surfaces (living or dead biomass), without requiring active metabolism
Conversion of metals into gaseous form
Complete destruction of the metal atoms
questions.correct_answer: Passive binding of metal ions to functional groups on microbial cell surfaces (living or dead biomass), without requiring active metabolism
questions.explanation: Biosorption is a largely passive, metabolism-independent process in which metal ions bind to reactive groups (carboxyl, hydroxyl, phosphate, amine) on microbial cell wall surfaces, allowing even non-living biomass to sequester metals.

questions.question: Some bacteria detoxify mercury compounds via the mer operon, which encodes mercuric reductase that:
options: Converts toxic organic mercury compounds into more toxic forms
Reduces the more toxic ionic mercury (Hg2+) to volatile, less reactive elemental mercury (Hg0), which can diffuse out of the cell
Permanently binds mercury inside the cell wall
Converts mercury into a solid precipitate that accumulates in the cytoplasm
questions.correct_answer: Reduces the more toxic ionic mercury (Hg2+) to volatile, less reactive elemental mercury (Hg0), which can diffuse out of the cell
questions.explanation: Mercuric reductase, encoded by the mer operon in mercury-resistant bacteria, reduces Hg2+ to metallic Hg0, which is far less reactive and can volatilise out of the cell, representing a bacterial detoxification mechanism exploited in bioremediation.

questions.question: Xenobiotic compounds, a major focus of biodegradation studies, are defined as:
options: Naturally occurring compounds found in all ecosystems
Synthetic or foreign chemical compounds, such as many pesticides and industrial pollutants, that are not naturally produced by living organisms and may be resistant to biodegradation
Compounds produced exclusively by bacteria
Simple sugars used in microbial growth media
questions.correct_answer: Synthetic or foreign chemical compounds, such as many pesticides and industrial pollutants, that are not naturally produced by living organisms and may be resistant to biodegradation
questions.explanation: Xenobiotics are man-made compounds foreign to biological systems; because many microorganisms have not evolved specific enzymes for them, xenobiotics such as certain pesticides and industrial chemicals can be recalcitrant (resistant) to biodegradation.

questions.question: Co-metabolism, relevant to the microbial degradation of some recalcitrant xenobiotics, refers to:
options: Two or more organisms competing directly for the same nutrient
Transformation of a compound by a microorganism that cannot use that compound as an energy or carbon source, occurring incidentally during metabolism of a different growth substrate
The complete mineralisation of a pollutant to CO2 and water by a single enzyme
Metabolism that only occurs in the absence of any other carbon source
questions.correct_answer: Transformation of a compound by a microorganism that cannot use that compound as an energy or carbon source, occurring incidentally during metabolism of a different growth substrate
questions.explanation: In co-metabolism, enzymes induced for degrading a primary growth substrate fortuitously also transform a structurally similar xenobiotic that cannot itself support the organism's growth, a mechanism important in degrading some persistent pollutants.

questions.question: Organochlorine pesticides such as DDT are generally more persistent (recalcitrant) in the environment than organophosphate pesticides mainly because:
options: They are more soluble in water
Their halogenated (chlorine-substituted) structure is not readily recognised or cleaved by common microbial degradative enzymes, and they tend to be lipophilic and accumulate in fatty tissue
They are broken down instantly by sunlight
They contain no carbon atoms
questions.correct_answer: Their halogenated (chlorine-substituted) structure is not readily recognised or cleaved by common microbial degradative enzymes, and they tend to be lipophilic and accumulate in fatty tissue
questions.explanation: Chlorine substitution on organic molecules like DDT often confers resistance to common microbial enzymes, slowing biodegradation; combined with high lipophilicity, this leads to environmental persistence and bioaccumulation up the food chain.

questions.question: Municipal solid waste management follows a widely recognised hierarchy of preferred approaches. From most to least preferred, this hierarchy generally places:
options: Disposal (landfilling) above waste reduction and recycling
Waste reduction/prevention and reuse above recycling, with recycling above treatment/recovery, and disposal (landfilling) as the least preferred option
Incineration as always the first choice
Composting always ranked below landfilling
questions.correct_answer: Waste reduction/prevention and reuse above recycling, with recycling above treatment/recovery, and disposal (landfilling) as the least preferred option
questions.explanation: The commonly taught waste management hierarchy prioritises preventing waste generation and reuse first, followed by recycling/composting, then energy recovery/treatment, with landfilling as the last resort due to its environmental costs.

questions.question: Which of the following best distinguishes biodegradable municipal solid waste from non-biodegradable waste?
options: Biodegradable waste (e.g. food scraps, paper, garden waste) can be broken down by microbial action into simpler, generally harmless compounds, while non-biodegradable waste (e.g. most plastics, glass) resists microbial decomposition
Biodegradable waste is always more hazardous than non-biodegradable waste
Non-biodegradable waste always dissolves in water
There is no practical difference between the two categories
questions.correct_answer: Biodegradable waste (e.g. food scraps, paper, garden waste) can be broken down by microbial action into simpler, generally harmless compounds, while non-biodegradable waste (e.g. most plastics, glass) resists microbial decomposition
questions.explanation: The biodegradable/non-biodegradable distinction underlies waste sorting and treatment strategy: organic materials can be composted or digested by microorganisms, while conventional plastics, metals, and glass persist and require recycling or other disposal routes.

questions.question: Certain microorganisms, notably strains of Ideonella sakaiensis, have attracted research interest in waste management because they can:
options: Produce large amounts of methane from glass waste
Enzymatically degrade polyethylene terephthalate (PET) plastic using enzymes such as PETase
Fix carbon dioxide into fossil fuels
Convert heavy metals into harmless gases
questions.correct_answer: Enzymatically degrade polyethylene terephthalate (PET) plastic using enzymes such as PETase
questions.explanation: Ideonella sakaiensis was identified for its ability to use PETase and MHETase enzymes to break down PET plastic into its monomeric building blocks, generating interest in microbial/enzymatic plastic biodegradation and recycling.

questions.question: Phytoremediation, often used alongside microbial bioremediation strategies, refers to:
options: The use of plants (sometimes together with their associated rhizosphere microorganisms) to remove, degrade, or stabilise contaminants in soil or water
The use of fungi exclusively to degrade pollutants
A method of physically excavating contaminated soil
Chemical precipitation of pollutants using acids
questions.correct_answer: The use of plants (sometimes together with their associated rhizosphere microorganisms) to remove, degrade, or stabilise contaminants in soil or water
questions.explanation: Phytoremediation employs plants, often in synergy with rhizosphere microbial communities that enhance pollutant uptake or degradation, to extract, sequester, or detoxify contaminants such as heavy metals and some organics.

questions.question: Bioaugmentation and biostimulation strategies at a bioremediation site are both typically most effective when environmental factors such as pH, temperature, moisture, and nutrient availability are:
options: Left completely uncontrolled
Monitored and optimised, since microbial degradative activity is highly sensitive to these physicochemical conditions
Irrelevant to microbial degradation rates
Only relevant for anaerobic processes
questions.correct_answer: Monitored and optimised, since microbial degradative activity is highly sensitive to these physicochemical conditions
questions.explanation: Because microbial growth and enzymatic activity depend strongly on pH, temperature, moisture, oxygen, and nutrient balance, successful bioremediation programmes routinely monitor and adjust these parameters to maximise pollutant degradation rates.
